slides.body: How to connect marketing data, analytics and custom software into automation that grows with the business, shown through two real projects.

slides.title: About me
slides.name: Blagovest Iordanov
slides.role: Data strategy, analytics infrastructure and technical implementation.

bullets.title: Background
points: Co-founder of ID – Digital Consulting, a performance digital agency focused on data-driven decisions in advertising
Translating each client's business goals into measurable marketing systems
This past year: AI agents that write and maintain the code for me

blocks.text: Every client is different. Their data isn't (mostly).

cards.label: The client
cards.title: Specific every time
cards.body: A unique business vision, markets and history, which produce a specific set of KPIs and goals.

cards.label: The data
cards.title: Similar underneath
cards.body: Platforms differ, but the raw data is strikingly similar: the same shape, the same dimensions and metrics, the same business logic. Businesses in the same industry end up with an almost identical semantic layer.

cards.label: The concept
cards.title: Build the structure once
cards.body: The differences are small and belong in configuration. The shared structure can be modelled once and reused.

blocks.label: The challenge
blocks.title: The way digital marketing does ETL and analysis is obsolete
blocks.body: Current tools and habits don't scale easily. Enter AI.

blocks.text: ETL and analysis: Current State

paragraphs: How does digital marketing get and analyse its data today? Each approach solves something, and each one breaks somewhere.

cards.label: 01 · Interface
cards.title: Google Ads UI
pros: Quick spot checks
Flat learning curve, at least at the start
cons: Painful UI; effort just to set up a view

cards.label: 02 · Exports
cards.title: Exports & dashboards
pros: Reliable source, hard to get wrong
Flat learning curve
Easy to share

cards.label: 03 · Spreadsheets
cards.title: Sheets via API / add-ons
pros: First real programmatic automation
Flexible formulas + JavaScript (Apps Script)
cons: Locked to the current data shape

cards.label: 04 · Connectors
cards.title: Third-party data connectors
pros: Rich functionality
Manageable learning curve
Quick to start
cons: Costly, priced per source or account

cards.label: 05 · AI
cards.title: AI prompts + MCP
pros: Plain-language questions
Live data, no pipeline
Great for exploration

slides.title: Can we build the tools we were missing?

blocks.text: Can we build the tools we were missing?

paragraphs: Every limit on the previous slide is a tooling problem. AI agents can now write, run and maintain that tooling, so fixing it no longer needs a data engineering team.

cards.label: vs. one client at a time
cards.title: Programmatic data access
cards.body: Every platform through its API or native export, for every client, on a schedule.

cards.label: vs. fragile scripts
cards.title: Pipelines built and maintained
cards.body: The agent writes extraction, transformation and tests, and fixes them when an API changes.

cards.label: vs. costly connectors
cards.title: Lower cost
cards.body: Pay for cloud usage, not per-source licences.

cards.label: vs. steep learning
cards.title: Manageable learning curve
cards.body: You describe the goal and the rules; the agent writes the code. You need to know the data, not how to code.

cards.label: vs. scattered data
cards.title: Ready for AI analysis
cards.body: Clean, documented, tested data in one warehouse is what AI needs to give reliable answers.

blocks.label: The shift
blocks.title: From buying tools to building your own
blocks.body: Tailored to your clients, owned by you, and better every time you use them.

slides.title: Why MCP alone isn't the answer

blocks.text: Why MCP alone isn't the answer

paragraphs: Given raw access, the model improvises its own analytical approach every time. The quality of the answer depends on the instructions and guardrails we give it.

items.text: No pipeline needed, set up in minutes
Great for exploration and finding gaps: it's how we found 291 days of cost mismatch
Row caps: a capped result can look complete
Not repeatable: the same question, computed differently each time
No history or memory: nothing scheduled or monitored
Subtle errors: averaged rates, mixed currencies, gaps read as zero

blocks.title: What it needs: instructions and guardrails

items.text: A semantic layer: which metrics, at which grain, how ratios are calculated
Written business rules: revenue, attribution, currencies, time zones
Checks before any number is shown: reconciliation, coverage, freshness
Instructions that persist: AGENTS.md, contracts, skills

blocks.label: The difference
blocks.title: Use AI to build the pipeline, not to be the pipeline.
blocks.body: The agent writes, tests and maintains the system. The system produces the numbers, visualisations and analyses.

blocks.text: Our approach in five ideas

cards.title: One schema, many clients
cards.body: Differences live in config, not in copies.

cards.title: The warehouse is the source of truth
cards.body: Exports and APIs land in BigQuery, with provenance.

cards.title: Code in repos, written by AI
cards.body: The repo is the memory: contracts, decisions, tests.

cards.title: Connectors for exploration
cards.body: MCP finds gaps; in production only under a contract.

cards.title: Verify before publishing
cards.body: Reconcile, test, and show "missing" instead of zero.

blocks.text: The process: from raw data to full automation

paragraphs: Five steps we repeat for every client. Each one makes the next client cheaper, and together they lead to the end game.

steps.title: Raw data, a step away
steps.body: Identical data shape, synced into BigQuery by Google DTS.

steps.title: Context discovery
steps.body: Each client's business, written down as a semantic library.

steps.title: Adapt templates
steps.body: Reporting and UI templates, applied through the library.

steps.title: Maintainable pipelines
steps.body: Automated QA and data quality first, humans in the loop.

steps.title: Client feedback loop
steps.body: Every round of feedback refines the library.

steps.title: Full automation
steps.body: Data, analysis and alerts run themselves. People make the decisions.

slides.title: Step 1: Raw data with identical shape, a step away

blocks.text: Step 1 · Raw data with identical shape, a step away

paragraphs: Google already delivers the raw data in the same shape for every account. Our job is not to extract it, but to manage it.

pros: DTS does the heavy lifting: daily sync and historical backfill
We pay only for storage and the queries we run
All data is already there: new reports and views need no new extraction
The same tables for every client: build once, reuse everywhere

todo: A wrapper that manages which accounts sync, and under which conditions
A QA suite that catches what goes wrong: lost permissions, failed or late transfers, accounts dropping out
A monitor for Google Ads API and schema changes

blocks.alt: BigQuery gads_raw dataset with Google Ads transfer tables
blocks.title: gads_raw in BigQuery: every Google Ads table, synced daily by DTS
blocks.caption: 94 accounts in one config table · freshness gate before every build · alert when an account drops out

blocks.text: In practice

pros: Google Ads DTS syncs every account into BigQuery daily
94 accounts configured (39 active) in one config table; stale accounts are excluded, not silently dropped
An account-sync wrapper acts as the export and backfill gate

todo: Automated data tests on every run: 155 checks for duplicates, gaps and currency coverage
Freshness alerts: a stale account is excluded and reported with its lag
Pipeline health check with an error resolver
API checks

notes: Reports are in EUR; accounts spend in BGN, USD, GBP, RON, MXN
Daily ECB reference rates; BGN uses its fixed peg (1.95583)
Weekends and ECB holidays reuse the last published rate
Example: a 13-day ECB gap left USD/GBP accounts without EUR cost. The refresh now restarts from its last loaded date, so gaps heal themselves

blocks.alt: Telegram health report from the notifier bot
blocks.title: Notifications: the daily Telegram health report
blocks.caption: Accounts status, excluded accounts with their lag, and alerts by type. Client names blurred.

slides.title: Step 2: Context discovery → the client's semantic library

blocks.text: Step 2 · Context discovery → the client's semantic library

paragraphs: A templated discovery turns each client's business into written rules: the semantic library that the ETL applies to the raw data.

pros: Templates make discovery repeatable, but it still takes business development experience to ask the right questions
AI speeds discovery up a lot: it checks sources, finds gaps and drafts the questions
One written source of truth: revenue definition, migration dates, country rules, source precedence

todo: Create the discovery templates, and evolve them with every client
A process that formalises the answers into rules the pipeline can apply
Keep open questions visible until a human decides

notes: Healthcare client: the first commit was the discovery report, not code
It listed 9 gaps and 8 decisions for a human
The answers became CONTRACTS.md, read by the agent before every task

blocks.text: Step 3 · Adapt templates, don't rebuild

paragraphs: Three kinds of templates, adapted through the semantic library instead of built from scratch.

pros: Reporting templates: the business questions are finite, after all
UI templates: for a given set of data, there is a best way to show it
Learning: every client's feedback improves the templates for the next

todo: An AI-driven build process that applies the formalised discoveries to the raw data
Feed it past experience, structured as knowledge, tooling, business context and client hierarchy
QA at every step. Don't skip it.

notes: 17 shared reporting tables and the report hub, built for the exporter
Adapted into the healthcare client's dashboard in 2 days

slides.title: Step 4: Maintainable pipelines, automated QA, data quality

blocks.text: Step 4 · Maintainable pipelines, automated QA, data quality

paragraphs: Bad data in, bad data out. Analysis is easy today; data quality and context are not. This is the most important part of the job.

pros: Managed cloud services: Cloud Run jobs, Cloud Scheduler, Secret Manager, BigQuery. Your time is the most expensive resource
Monitoring that comes to you: a Telegram bot reports every run and every failure
Parse errors and retry only what is worth retrying
Scheduled AI tasks for holistic QA and pipeline reviews

todo: Publish only after checks pass; on failure, the client keeps the last good data
Reconcile against the source by account, campaign and day
Show freshness and coverage on every report; missing is never zero
Measure cost in bytes, and version every release for one-step rollback

notes: A new coverage test found a 13-day gap in ECB exchange rates
Reconciliation found a 0.44% cost mismatch in the shared export

slides.title: In practice: keeping it cheap and correct
slides.body: From the exporter's repo: the agent measures, proves nothing is lost, and a new test finds an old bug.

slides.title: Step 5: A feedback loop with the client

blocks.text: Step 5 · A feedback loop with the client

paragraphs: The first version is a hypothesis. The client's reaction turns it into a system they trust and use.

pros: Early previews: the client sees real data within days, not a spec
Feedback is written back into the semantic library, so it's never lost
Trust: definitions and data freshness are visible on every report
Better templates for the next client

todo: Short preview cycles with the people who will use the reports
One channel for feedback, and a record of what changed and why
Usage signals: which views get opened, which get ignored
Regular reviews as the business changes: new markets, campaigns, goals

notes: Healthcare client: preview feedback on filters, projections and comparisons applied the same day
A later decision made the final legacy export canonical

slides.title: How I organise knowledge and work

blocks.text: How I organise knowledge and work

paragraphs: Four layers. Each builds on the one before, and every new client adds back to the first three.

steps.title: Knowledge
steps.body: What we know: discovery templates, metric definitions, contracts, lessons and rejected ideas.

steps.title: Tooling
steps.body: What we build once: extractors, dbt models, the FX pipeline, QA suite, notifier, deploy scripts.

steps.title: Business cases
steps.body: Reusable solutions: Ads reporting, commerce + Ads ROAS, product feeds, tracking.

steps.title: Clients
steps.body: One repo per client: its semantic library and config, built from the layers above.

loop.label: Every client feeds back into knowledge and tooling

pros: Google Ads exporter, Shopify extractor, GTM extractor, product feed engine
Each one a repo, reused as a reference
cards.prosLabel: Tooling, in my GIT Projects folder

notes: Reads the tooling repos, never modifies them

blocks.text: Scaffolding that preserves project memory

paragraphs: An AI agent starts every session from zero. The repo is its memory, so these files come first.

cards.label: AGENTS.md
cards.title: Operating rules
cards.body: What to read first, what never to touch, where to deploy. "Do not modify any reference repository."

cards.label: docs/discovery
cards.title: What we found
cards.body: What was checked, what is missing, and the questions for a human.

cards.label: docs/decisions.md
cards.title: What was decided
cards.body: The answers, with dates. They supersede provisional notes.

cards.label: docs/CONTRACTS.md
cards.title: Rules to follow
cards.body: Revenue, source precedence, IDs, currency, access. Read before every change.

cards.label: Runbooks
cards.title: How to operate
cards.body: Deploy, backfill, recover. E.g. the FX backfill and the Ads import runbook.

cards.label: Commit history
cards.title: Why it changed
cards.body: One change, one commit, one reason: the timeline of every decision.

blocks.label: Rule of thumb
blocks.title: If a decision isn't written in the repo, the next session will undo it.

blocks.text: Why I work in code repositories

paragraphs: I don't write the code by hand. I write the tasks, decisions and rules. An AI agent (Codex, Claude Code) implements them in the repo, and Git keeps everything.

cards.title: History
cards.body: Every change is a commit with a reason. The exporter has 74, and each one says why, not just what.

cards.title: Memory
cards.body: AGENTS.md, contracts and decisions in docs/. The agent reads them before every task and doesn't repeat old mistakes.

cards.title: Tests
cards.body: Business rules become checks the agent must pass before anything ships. They catch its mistakes and ours: a new FX test found a 13-day gap. 155 data + 38 unit tests.

cards.title: Reuse
cards.body: A new project reads older repos as references but never changes them.

blocks.text: Read docs/CONTRACTS.md as durable project memory.

slides.title: Cloud or workflow platform
slides.body: It isn't either-or. The question is how much data there is, how often the rules change, and who will maintain it.

columns.label: Make / n8n / Zapier
columns.title: Workflow platform
items: Little data, event → action (lead → CRM → Slack)
Business users can change the steps themselves
Limits on operations and run time
Hard to test, hard to diff versions

columns.label: Cloud Run + BigQuery + dbt
columns.title: Cloud infrastructure
items: Hundreds of thousands of rows a day, years of history
Rules that must be verified (currencies, attribution, ROAS)
Tests, staging, rollback to a previous image
Cost measured in GB, not in task counts
The AI agent writes the code, so "hard to maintain" is no longer an argument

blocks.text: Practical tips for working with AI

cards.title: Discovery before code
cards.body: Let the agent inspect read-only first, and stop for decisions.

cards.title: Link layers, don't fork them
cards.body: Client repos read shared knowledge, tooling and business cases. Improvements go back to the shared layer, not into a copy.

cards.title: Measure before optimising
cards.body: Billed bytes, row counts, run times. Then change one thing.

cards.title: Keep humans on definitions
cards.body: Revenue, attribution, access: a person decides, the agent records.

cards.title: Write down trade-offs
cards.body: Record rejected ideas and why, so they aren't proposed again.

cards.title: Secrets stay out of Git
cards.body: Credentials in Secret Manager; tokens renewed, never saved.

cards.title: Make every run idempotent
cards.body: A rerun replaces the same dates, never appends. Rolling windows pick up late conversions.

cards.title: Check it like a user
cards.body: Open the report in a browser, not only the tests.

slides.title: The trust boundary
slides.body: AI prepares, executes and verifies. A human decides what the data means for the business.
slides.boundary: AI builds and proves; the human sets the rules

ai.label: The AI agent does
items: Discovery of sources, schemas and gaps
Reconciliation to the cent and A/B checks
Documents every decision in the repo

human.label: The human decides
items: The migration date and which source takes precedence
Who gets access to the client's data
Whether to trade a safety stage for a 50% lower bill
